title: Indian Oil will buy its own crude and LPG ships to beat rising freight costs
subtitle: Hiring a ship for one trip now costs up to five times more than a long rental, so India's biggest refiner wants a fleet of its own.
content_html:
Picture a ship full of cooking gas. In normal times, carrying one tonne of that gas to India costs about $40. Today, on the open market, the same trip can cost $160 to $180. That is four times the old price, or more. On 8 November 2026, India's biggest oil refiner, Indian Oil Corporation, said it plans to buy its own crude oil and LPG carrier ships, so the company depends less on renting them.

The news came from Anuj Jain, the company's Director of Finance, on its second quarter earnings call. An earnings call is a meeting where a company explains its latest three months of results to people who study and invest in it. He said the board has already approved buying a few vessels, and tenders were issued several months ago. A tender is a public invitation asking shipbuilders and sellers to offer their best price.

First, what are freight costs?

Freight is the money paid to carry goods from one place to another. When a samosa seller pays an auto driver to bring a sack of potatoes from the market, that fare is freight. For India's oil companies, the sack of potatoes is crude oil or LPG, and the auto is a giant ship crossing the sea.

Crude oil is raw oil pumped out of the ground. Refineries turn it into petrol, diesel and other fuels. LPG is the cooking gas that fills the red cylinders in Indian kitchens. India buys a lot of both from abroad, so it pays a lot of freight. According to Maritime Gateway, India imports roughly 60% of its LPG, much of it from the Gulf, for a fuel used by more than 300 million households.

Freight is measured per barrel for crude oil and per tonne for LPG. A barrel is a standard drum size used across the world to count oil.

Why did ship fares jump?

Oil prices rose sharply after fighting between the US and Iran grew worse towards the end of February, the PTI report said. Since then, trouble around the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route near the Gulf, has pushed up ship fares and the cost of war risk insurance. That insurance is extra cover that ship owners buy before sailing through dangerous waters, and the cost lands on whoever hires the ship.

Jain said India's crude basket, a mix of crude prices that India tracks, averaged about $65 to $70 a barrel in February. It stayed above $100 for much of the first quarter and averaged about $120 a barrel in October.

Taxi or scooter: three ways to move oil

Think about getting to college every day. There are three choices.

  • Hail a taxi each time. You pay whatever today's fare is. On a rainy day with surge pricing, the fare can jump four times. In shipping, this is the spot market: hiring a ship for one trip at that day's price.
  • Book a monthly cab. You agree on a fixed fare for months. In shipping, this is a time charter: renting a ship for a set period at an agreed rate.
  • Buy your own scooter. It costs a lot on day one, but no surge pricing can touch you after that. This is owning the ship.

Indian Oil has mostly lived in the first two worlds. Its shipping has relied on a mix of time charter and single trip ships, the report said. Right now it has three crude oil vessels and nine LPG vessels on time charter, and Jain said these deals have saved the company a lot of money during the crisis.

Here is how big that saving is. Indian Oil's time chartered crude carriers cost around $2 to $2.50 a barrel. On the spot market, the same job costs as much as $8 to $10 a barrel. So the taxi fare is roughly three to five times the monthly cab fare.

What Indian Oil plans to do now

The company is looking at three paths, according to the report: getting better deals on the ships it already rents, owning ships, and supporting shipbuilding in India. Jain said Indian Oil is also exploring building ships in India under the government's Make in India programme.

"The country needs oil sector companies to focus more on the shipping area now," Jain said, the news agency PTI reported.

The company's chairman made a similar point on 27 October at an energy meet in Goa, Maritime Gateway reported, warning that high freight was eating up the discount India gets on the crude it buys.

Who is Indian Oil, anyway?

Indian Oil was founded on 30 June 1959. It is owned by the Government of India and has its head office in New Delhi. It refines crude, runs pipelines, and sells petrol, diesel and LPG across the country.

It has also been changing where it buys oil. In the first half of this financial year, 55% of its crude came from Russia and 24% from the Middle East, Jain said. About 87% of its crude was bought on the spot market in that period, up from around 50% the year before. To stay safe, it has raised its crude stock to about 39 days of use, from its usual 33 to 35 days, and it holds 20 days of LPG.

What could this change for India?

Owning ships does not make oil cheaper overnight. Ships take time to buy or build, and the board has approved only a few. But the idea is simple. When a refiner owns some of its ships, a part of its freight bill stops jumping every time the sea gets risky. Like a scooter in the monsoon, the ride costs the same whether the taxi fare surges or not.

That matters for everyone. Freight is part of what India pays for every barrel of crude and every tonne of LPG it brings home. Steadier freight means the oil company has a clearer idea of its costs. It also means India has more control over getting fuel home on time, instead of waiting for a ship owner to say yes.

Jain also warned that events in the region remain a big source of uncertainty, because they affect buying crude, freight and the money made on selling fuel.
